summary.text: An earthquake is shaking of Earth's surface caused by a sudden release of energy in the lithosphere that sends out seismic waves.
Most come from faults: rough spots lock the two sides together, stress builds as the plates keep moving, and the fault suddenly slips once that stress breaks through.
Only about 10 percent or less of the energy leaves as seismic waves; most powers the growth of the fracture or turns into frictional heat.

items.prompt: You drag a heavy box across a rough floor: it holds still, holds still, then lurches forward all at once. Which fault behaviour does this resemble?

options.label: Locking at rough spots, then sudden release
Smooth sliding with no friction at all
Rock melting under the moving plates
Steady creep at a constant speed

items.explain: Rough spots on most faults cause stick-slip behaviour: the fault locks, stress builds, then it suddenly slides.

items.prompt: Imagine a fault whose two faces are perfectly smooth, with no rough spots. What would you expect?

options.label: Larger earthquakes than normal
Smooth sliding with no earthquakes
No movement of the sides at all
Sudden jolts every few seconds

items.explain: The sides of a fault slide past each other smoothly and without quakes only when no irregularities add friction.

items.prompt: When a fault suddenly slips, where does most of the released energy go?

options.label: Into shaking the ground as seismic waves
Into lifting mountains a little higher
Into breaking rock and frictional heat
Into pushing water up as tsunamis

items.explain: Only about 10 percent or less is radiated as seismic energy; most drives fracture growth or becomes frictional heat.

items.prompt: A quake begins rupturing 20 kilometres beneath a town. What is the spot on the ground directly over that starting point called?

options.label: The focus
The fault trace
The hypocenter
The epicenter

items.explain: The rupture starts at the hypocenter, or focus, and the ground-level point straight above it is the epicenter.

items.prompt: The deadliest earthquakes in history were not all the most powerful ones. What mainly made them so deadly?

options.label: Being close to crowded areas or the ocean
Lasting far longer than other quakes
Striking deep under the ocean floor
Happening in very cold weather

items.explain: The most lethal quakes were deadly because they struck near dense populations or the ocean, where they often cause tsunamis.

items.prompt: Two regions face the same strong quake. Where is the risk of great loss of life highest?

options.label: Where quakes are frequent and codes strict
Where few people live near the fault
Where quakes are rare and codes are lax
Where the ground is solid bedrock

items.explain: The greatest risk is where earthquakes are rare but powerful, and in poor regions with weak or unenforced building codes.
